old_entry.title: Bertie the Brain
old_entry.subtitle: An engineer gives the public an opponent
old_entry.summary: Josef Kates used a familiar game to introduce an unfamiliar machine at the Canadian National Exhibition.
body: In Toronto in 1950, visitors could challenge a machine at tic-tac-toe. Josef Kates built Bertie the Brain for the Canadian National Exhibition, using a keypad for the player's moves and a large illuminated display to show the contest. Its adjustable difficulty let the same installation offer different levels of resistance.

Kates was also demonstrating his Additron tube, an electronic component he had developed. A game gave that engineering a public face: instead of asking visitors to understand a circuit, Bertie asked them to make a move. The component did not become a commercial successor to conventional vacuum tubes, but the demonstration remains an early example of a computer opponent presented to ordinary visitors.

Bertie used lamps rather than a video screen. That distinction matters when comparing it with later experiments. It belongs in the origins of electronic play without needing to win a single, universal contest for the title of first video game.

editorial_features.title: A game in front of the crowd
editorial_features.summary: Kates connected experimental electronics with a contest anyone could follow.
body: Kates reached computing through several kinds of machinery. In his 1992 interview, he remembered studying mathematics and physics in Toronto while also working at Rogers Majestic. Radio tubes were part of his paid employment; experimental computing became another place to apply that knowledge. This was not a games company recruiting a games designer. A university researcher and an electronics manufacturer were approaching a shared technical problem. Bertie emerged from that connection, before anyone involved needed a videogame department or a market category to explain the project.

The machine presented two views of the contest: a small board for the player and a larger illuminated board for the watching crowd. Kates recalled adjustable difficulty and a version of tic-tac-toe that could punish a mistaken move. He also remembered Harry Stein helping with construction at Rogers. Kates dated this exhibition encounter to 1951. People had to see whose turn it was, understand the result and believe that another attempt might go differently. The public display made a private decision visible to everyone standing nearby.

Rogers hoped the installation would draw attention to the Additron, a binary adder tube. The Canada Science and Technology Museum’s research places it within efforts to build UTEC at the University of Toronto. Technical difficulties kept the component from becoming part of that full-scale computer; Bertie instead became its special-purpose demonstration. For the manufacturer, the game advertised an electronic device. For a visitor, the device disappeared behind the much simpler question of where to place the next mark. Those purposes occupied the same cabinet.

The museum monograph dates Bertie’s Canadian National Exhibition appearance to 1950 and reproduces a photograph in its account of early Canadian computing. Its detailed caption traces that image through John Vardalas’s research to a Rogers Majestic publication. That chain matters: the picture is evidence of an installation, not a newly made reconstruction or an openly licensed museum illustration. Beside the game, the Additron belongs to a larger history of machines that did not develop as planned. The record shows both the public attraction and the engineering ambition behind it.
